documents.title: AMSSM Position Statement on Concussion in Sport

chunks.content: INTRODUCTION Approximately 60 to 70 million cases of traumatic brain injury (TBI) occur worldwide annually, with 73% to 90% classified as mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI). Due to its high prevalence and frequently underestimated sequelae, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention considers concussion a major public health concern. Vestibular symptoms are common following TBI. Peripheral vestibular structures can be damaged at the level of the labyrinth or the vestibular nerve. Post-concussive vestibular dysfunction (PCVD) results from damage to peripheral structures (labyrinth or vestibular nerve) and central pathways within the brainstem, cerebellum, and supratentorial vestibular cortex. Although macrostructural damage is rarer in mTBI than in moderate and severe TBI, microstructural white matter abnormalities and diffuse axonal injury are frequently reported. In pediatric and sports medicine, the prevalence of vestibular dysfunction reaches up to 81%, with dizziness reported by 67%–77% of patients during the acute phase. It is well documented that initial presentation of dizziness is one predictor of a protracted recovery following concussion. The functional scope of the vestibular system extends beyond mere visual and balance control to encompass various domains such as self-orientation, sensory organization, and sensory weighting. The complexity of PCVD may also be associated with cervical or temporomandibular joint dysfunction. This review investigates the mechanisms, assessment, and differential diagnosis of PCVD, alongside evidence-based rehabilitation protocols and the latest advancements in technology, aiming to provide clinical insights to maximize patient recovery. MECHANISMS AND PATHOPHYSIOLOGY illustrates a brief schematic of the integrated pathophysiology. Peripheral vestibular injury Peripheral vestibular disorders range from common conditions such as benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) to less common causes including labyrinthine concussion, perilymphatic fistulas, endolymphatic hydrops, and temporal bone fractures. Other less common conditions are post-traumatic Meniere’s syndrome and direct damage to the vestibular nerve itself. Inferior vestibular nerve damage, often resulting from traumatic nerve stretching, is a frequently overlooked mechanism of PCVD. While difficult to detect via conventional exams, it can be elucidated through vestibular evoked myogenic potentials and high-precision imaging; thus, clinical suspicion should warrant otolaryngologic referral for accurate diagnosis. Furthermore, otolith organs may be more vulnerable to mTBI than semicircular canals, leading to severe dizziness even with normal vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR) tests. In such cases, specialized rehabilitation focusing on postural control and spatial orientation must be integrated with conventional VOR-based exercises to optimize recovery. Central vestibular injury Anatomically, the vestibular system connects inner ear organs with the brainstem, cerebellum, and the parieto-insular vestibular cortex (PIVC), linking closely with the ocular system and postural muscles. Concussions cause extensive microstructural disruption of white matter channels including the cerebellar peduncles rather than localized lesions. Previous imaging has demonstrated volume reduction in the brainstem and decreased fractional anisotropy in the corpus callosum, leading to pervasive damage in networks regulating vestibulo-ocular and vestibulo-spinal reflexes (VSRs). Higher-order vestibular functions are mediated by complex networks integrating multisensory information with feedback and feedforward cognitive control. Vestibular signals project beyond the frontal and parietal lobes to the medial temporal lobe and hippocampus, forming a comprehensive cerebral connectivity that is often disrupted in PCVD. As the cerebellum, especially vestibulocerebellum, is a critical structure that regulates motor responses by integrating vestibular, visual, and proprioceptive inputs, dysfunction in this region leads to persistent imbalance, dizziness, and gaze instability. Furthermore, the frontal lobe, which is highly vulnerable to concussive forces, governs higher-order oculomotor control. Deficits in the spatial mapping process—a critical precursor to conscious attention—lead to reduced accuracy and efficiency in both saccades and smooth pursuits. Dysfunctional sensory integration and pathological visual dependency Normal balance relies on the dynamic modulation of multisensory inputs. However, patients with chronic mTBI often struggle with central sensory integration. Unlike those in the acute phase, chronic PCVD patients fail to preferentially process vestibular and somatosensory signals when visual information is unavailable. This suggests that visual dependency in chronic mTBI is a long-term deficit in multisensory processing rather than a simple compensatory strategy, likely due to disrupted connectivity within the PIVC and multisensory hubs. Furthermore, post-concussion hyperactivation of the visual cortex and abnormal vestibulo-limbic interactions via the parabrachial nucleus can exacerbate the psychological fixation of dizziness, potentially transitioning acute instability into persistent post-concussive symptoms (PPCS) or chronic phobic postural vertigo. These mechanisms underscore why active sensory reorganization—rather than simple symptom-suppressing medication—is essential for mTBI recovery. While vestibular suppressants provide temporary relief, they may hinder neuroplasticity. Conversely, habituation and sensory re-weighting training facilitate the resolution of pathological visual dependency and restructure damaged PIVC connectivity. By promoting neural adaptation through repetitive exposure, these strategies optimize multisensory integration and prevent progression into chronic psychogenic vertigo. Additionally, central vestibular injury may cause vestibular agnosia, where the brain fails to recognize body movement. This can lead to frequent falls and clinical oversight, as patients may be unaware of their dysfunction. Therefore, evaluating PCVD requires a comprehensive approach that correlates objective test results with subjective reports.

Cervicogenic contributions to PCVD Concussive acceleration-deceleration forces often cause cervical spine injuries, such as whiplash. The upper cervical spine possesses a high density of muscle spindles, and traumatic changes—including inflammation and fatty infiltration—alter their sensitivity. This distortion of proprioceptive afferent information results in sensory mismatch, which is further exacerbated by chronic neck pain and sympathetic activation. Consequently, a vicious cycle of persistent pain and postural instability develops. These ‘false signals’ originating from the neck, the body’s balance control system misses the proper timing, causing confusion in the information integration process. This interference with the tuning of the VOR and VSR can lead to secondary gaze instability, and visual disturbance, causing patients to experience an unstable visual field and difficulty with fixation. Psychological dimensions and persistent positional-perceptual dizziness (PPPD) PPPD is a chronic vestibular dysfunction characterized by impaired central processing of balance information following concussion or whiplash, accounting for 10%–15% of all PPPD cases. Beyond non-rotational vertigo—often described as cloudiness or heaviness—patients suffer from persistent instability and hypersensitivity to visual and somatosensory stimuli. The core mechanism involves the brain misinterpreting ordinary environmental stimuli as 'danger,' leading to a sustained, maladaptive vertigo response. Clinicians frequently overlook the critical interplay between vestibular anxiety and kinesiophobia in PPPD patients during routine evaluations. These psychological factors are not merely secondary; they actively exacerbate vestibular symptoms via neural circuits that bridge the amygdala, the limbic system, and the vestibular nuclei. Notably, those struggling with kinesiophobia often resort to protective avoidance behaviors, such as rigid head fixation. Such immobilization effectively mutes the 'sensory-error signals' that the brain relies on for self-calibration. By depriving the nervous system of these essential inputs, this restriction directly stalls habituation and adaptation—the very pillars of vestibular compensation—thereby anchoring the patient in a state of delayed recovery. In the post-concussion context, PPPD may arise de novo from disrupted sensory reweighting or be directly precipitated by the acute vestibular event itself. Alternatively, the condition may be precipitated by the acute vestibular insult itself. Therefore, clinicians should maintain a high index of suspicion for PPPD in patients presenting with chronic, treatment-resistant dizziness, particularly when symptoms are exacerbated by visually demanding environments or sustained upright posture. NATURAL HISTORY AND PROGNOSIS PCVD typically improves during the acute phase; however, approximately one-third of untreated athletes with mTBI develop chronic symptoms. Moreover, as physiological vestibular dysfunction may persist even after subjective symptoms subside, careful follow-up is essential. The cognitive and emotional symptoms and reduced occupational performance associated with PPCS-often exacerbated by persistent PCVD-compromise social roles, causing patients to experience a ‘loss of self’ and significant changes in identity. Notably, the TRACK-TBI study confirmed that 26% of patients reported persistent symptoms even one year post-injury, suggesting that long-term PCVD is by no means a rare sequela and warrants targeted intervention. Early clinical evidence of vestibular-oculomotor dysfunction is associated with a 4-fold increased risk of developing persistent symptoms. Factors such as impaired VOR, a history of concussion, underlying psychiatric disorders, and onset in female patients are closely associated with delayed recovery. These findings emphasize that PCVD is a marker of substantial functional impairment rather than a mere subjective complaint. Therefore, determining a safe return to daily activities or sports should be based on objective evaluations of vestibular function than relying solely on the patient's self-reports. Cervicogenic contributions are also important prognostic markers, because cervical symptoms affect up to 90% of chronic mTBI patients. Initial neck pain increases the risk of prolonged recovery, often due to sensory mismatch where distorted proprioceptive signals from the injured upper cervical spine conflict with visual and vestibular inputs. This disharmony often involves cervical strain and impaired central sensory integration, can lead to maladaptive sensory reweighting if not addressed early. The pattern of nystagmus is a key indicator for differential diagnosis: horizontal and direction-fixed nystagmus suggest unilateral peripheral vestibular dysfunction. Conversely, vertical or rotational nystagmus, or gaze-evoked nystagmus indicates a central lesion. Utilizing Frenzel lenses or video nystagmography enhance diagnostic reliability. For sport-related concussions, the Vestibular Ocular Motor Screening efficiently evaluate smooth pursuit, saccades, near point of convergence, VOR, and visual motion sensitivity, serving as a valuable predictor of recovery duration. Additionally, the King-Devick Test provides a rapid screening for saccadic eye movements and suboptimal brain function through timed rapid number naming. Assessment of static and dynamic balance is essential to determine functional status. Standard measures include the Sensory Organization Test, which measures integration abilities, its simplified version, modified Clinical Test of Sensory Interaction on Balance, and the Balance Error Scoring System (BESS). However, the BESS may have low discriminative power for high-level athletes due to the ceiling effect. Dynamic balance and gait function can be evaluated using the tandem gait task and motion analysis. Patient-reported outcomes are captured using the Dizziness Handicap Inventory (DHI), which quantifies functional, emotional, and physical impacts of symptoms. Advanced diagnostic tests or imaging such as video head impulse test, vestibular evoked myogenic potential, and magnetic resonance imaging, are not routinely indicated, they should be considered for worsening symptoms, inconclusive bedside findings, or suspected structural lesions. Differential diagnosis Differential diagnosis of vestibular dysfunction and dizziness following mTBI are summarized in . It is important to note that whiplash injury, concussion, and cervicogenic dizziness are not mutually exclusive diagnoses and often coexist. As no “gold standard” exists for cervicogenic dizziness, diagnosis relies on both the exclusion of other neuro-otological disorders and the presence of clinical findings such as neck pain, restricted range of motion (ROM), cervical tenderness, and dizziness induced by passive neck rotation. Consequently, a basic cervical examination—assessing pain, ROM, and radiculopathy—should precede the full vestibular workup. If cervical movement is limited, subsequent vestibular tests must be modified accordingly. The head-neck differentiation test (seated cervical rotation test) is a useful tool for distinguishing cervicogenic from vestibular components. If dizziness is elicited by rotating the torso while the head remains fixed (using a swivel chair), a cervical origin is suspected; conversely, dizziness during simultaneous head and torso rotation suggests a vestibular etiology. In the chronic phase, differentiation is crucial because patients with vestibular migraine or PPPD are highly sensitive to visual stimuli. PRINCIPLES OF VESTIBULAR REHABILITATION: ADAPTATION, SUBSTITUTION, AND HABITUATION Symptoms of vestibular dysfunction, such as nystagmus and postural asymmetry, often resolve through central vestibular compensation. This process involves the central nervous system's plasticity to re-establish equilibrium between bilateral vestibular nuclei. While spontaneous recovery is common, targeted VRT is indicated for persistent PCVD. Notably, acute-phase medications can suppress the central nervous system, hindering neuroplasticity; thus, minimizing drug use and encouraging early activity are crucial. VRT is fundamentally based on three pillars: adaptation, substitution, and habituation ( ). In bilateral vestibular loss, the cervico-ocular reflex provides limited compensation (typically ≤0.5 Hz). Therefore, for high-frequency stability (e.g., walking), combining adaptive training to maximize residual function is more effective than relying solely on substitution. Beyond these fundamental pillars, specific strategies are required for cerebellar lesions and vestibular disinhibition. Since the cerebellum acts as an 'inhibitory brake' on vestibular output, its impairment often results in VOR disinhibition. In such cases, VOR suppression training is essential to restore cerebellar regulation. Additionally, VOR memory training (remembered target training) can be implemented to enhance internal predictive models and spatial memory by having patients visualize targets during head movements with their eyes closed. VESTIBULAR REHABILITATION PRACTICE A patient-specific approach VRT must be tailored to specific functional deficits and symptom-provoking factors. The key is to adjust intensity according to symptom response and functional tolerance rather than adhering to a fixed schedule. While mild symptom induction is permissible, the treatment focuses on systematic adaptation through graded exposure within an acceptable range. Furthermore, VRT should be directly linked to functional goals (e.g., community ambulation, driving, or returning to sports) and monitored accordingly. Finally, optimal outcomes are achieved when VRT is implemented within a comprehensive multidisciplinary framework that includes patient education and pacing strategies. Recent guidelines (e.g., 2021 JAMA Network Open) suggest systematic information provision, progressive aerobic exercise, vestibular rehabilitation, and manual therapy for the non-pharmacological treatment of PPCS; however, the level of recommendation was weak due to low certainty of evidence. Importantly, a lack of objective improvement should prompt a multidisciplinary review of the diagnosis to prevent entrenching maladaptive illness behaviors, rather than simply extending existing exercises. Timing of referral and initiation The paradigm is shifting from traditional ‘symptom stabilization’ toward early intervention as soon as dysfunction is identified. Early referrals to vestibulo-ocular and cervicovestibular therapy can accelerate symptom resolution and return to sports. In adolescents, starting individualized rehabilitation within 21 days of onset has shown significantly superior recovery compared to simple observation. If no signs of natural recovery are observed during the subacute period, immediate referral is necessary to prevent chronicity. Clinicians must avoid ‘clinical inertia’—neglecting the condition when recovery deviates from the expected path. Therapeutic dosing in vestibular rehabilitation According to the updated clinical practice guidelines from the Academy of Neurologic Physical Therapy of the American Physical Therapy Association, patients with chronic unilateral vestibular hypofunction should perform balance exercises for at least 20 minutes daily for 4–6 weeks, and 6–9 weeks for bilateral cases. While the necessity of exercise is acknowledged for acute and subacute patients, specific dosage recommendations remain undefined. For gaze stabilization exercises, it is recommended that acute/subacute unilateral patients exercise for at least 12 minutes per day (divided into three sessions), while chronic unilateral patients should aim for at least 20 minutes per day (divided into 3 to 5 sessions) for 4 to 6 weeks. Notably, patients with bilateral vestibular hypofunction are advised to exercise for 20 to 40 minutes per day over 5 to 7 weeks. Previous research has noted that repeating brief unidirectional optokinetic stimulation for 30 seconds, approximately 10 times daily, can induce changes in VOR gain. This suggests that even short periods of stimulation, when performed repeatedly, can sufficiently promote the recovery of vestibular function. To enhance adherence, clinicians should integrate exercises into daily activities to mitigate boredom and discomfort. Cervicovestibular rehabilitation Manual therapy, particularly focused on the upper cervical spine, significantly improves dizziness intensity and its impact on daily life compared to control or placebo treatments. However, the level of evidence for other clinical indicators remains insufficient; the certainty of evidence for pain intensity, cervical ROM, and disability indices was assessed as ‘low’ or ‘very low.’ This suggests that while manual therapy effectively alleviates specific symptoms, further robust evidence is needed to confirm its overall clinical impact. Multimodal interventions—combining cervical manual therapy with vestibular and/or oculomotor exercises—are superior to monotherapy for achieving faster clinical improvement and return to sport, particularly in persistent cases. For instance, treating cervical dysfunction and BPPV within three weeks of injury, followed by visual-vestibular integration therapy, significantly improves both objective and subjective outcomes in patients with comorbid cervicogenic headache and vestibular deficits. However, cervicovestibular rehabilitation is not a panacea. A randomized clinical trial showed that adding this therapy to symptom-limited aerobic exercise provided no superior benefit in subjective symptoms (e.g., pain, dizziness, headache) or functional recovery speed compared to aerobic exercise alone. Conversely, the combined group showed a clear advantage in objective measures, such as VOR and craniovertebral mobility. Thus, concurrent cervicovestibular rehabilitation and VRT are specifically indicated for patients with confirmed VOR impairment or limited cervical mobility. Psychological and anxiety dimensions in PPPD Standard VRT protocols are often less effective for PPPD than for structural lesions, as many patients discontinue conventional habituation due to symptom exacerbation. This underscores the necessity of an anxiety-informed, modified rehabilitation approach. Baseline anxiety and depression are independent negative predictors of VRT outcomes; a higher psychological burden significantly attenuates functional recovery, as measured by the DHI. Evidence-based treatment for vestibular anxiety and PPPD requires a multifaceted approach. Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is designed to correct maladaptive beliefs and movement avoidance behaviors associated with dizziness. With follow-up results of up to six months, CBT significantly reduced DHI scores and anxiety levels. Therefore, if factors that may psychologically exacerbate PPPD patients are identified, CBT must be included as a core treatment element of VRT. Graded exposure—the systematic, desensitized reintroduction of symptom-provoking activities in a controlled, progressively challenging sequence—serves as the behavioral backbone of this approach. Meta-analytic evidence further supports that the combination of SSRIs or serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors with structured VRT yields superior outcomes in DHI score reduction and anxiety compared to either modality in isolation; however, current evidence from placebo-controlled randomized trials remains limited, necessitating individualized risk-benefit assessment for pharmacological adjuncts. These conditions should be managed through coordinated neuropsychiatric consultation, rather than simply escalating the exercise dose or extending treatment duration. EMERGING TECHNOLOGIES AND FUTURE DIRECTIONS Virtual reality (VR) VR platforms represent one of the most rapidly evolving fields in vestibular rehabilitation, effectively suppressing ‘visual vertigo’ by inducing habituation through exposure to complex visual environments. Although studies on concussion patients indicate that VR-based rehabilitation improves balance, gait, and functional outcomes, the overall quality of evidence is currently categorized as low. A recent meta-analysis indicates that VR-assisted therapy significantly improves DHI scores compared to conventional therapy, particularly in peripheral disorders; however, high heterogeneity and limited efficacy in central disorders necessitate further large-scale validation. To address these limitations, recent research has focused on enhancing ecological validity and objective monitoring. For instance, the Praxis system utilizes a military-specific VR framework combined with wearable sensors to detect subtle vestibular deficits that traditional assessments often miss. This technology-driven approach aims to optimize recovery tracking and refine return-to-duty criteria for service members with mTBI. Similarly, a case study of a collegiate football player demonstrated that a 10-week intervention using VR and force-plate technology significantly improved both objective stability and subjective post-concussion symptoms. These advancements illustrate the potential of immersive, data-driven platforms to provide standardized, high-sensitivity rehabilitation that bridges the gap between clinical settings and real-world functional demands. These advancements are further supported by the increasing accessibility of high-performance, cost-effective VR hardware, which has transitioned from specialized research tools to broader clinical application. Nevertheless, the current literature has yet to establish optimal patient selection, standardized treatment durations, or the definitive additive benefit of VR over well-designed conventional therapy. Wearables and biofeedback Wearable technology enables precise movement quantification and real-time feedback beyond clinical settings. For instance, the Vertigenius™ system utilizes a retroauricular sensor and mobile app to monitor eye stabilization exercises and manage dizziness indicators remotely. Similarly, audio biofeedback (ABF) systems provide auditory cues for postural correction; in chronic mTBI, an randomized controlled trial demonstrated that VR with ABF significantly enhances motor activation and reduces response time delays compared to standard therapy. Wearable inertial measurement units (IMUs) further provide an objective means to monitor home-based exercise quality. In 73 patients with mTBI, IMU-derived metrics revealed slower peak forehead angular velocity and increased ROM compared to controls, suggesting compensatory strategies and impaired proprioception, respectively. Building on this, the ongoing SuBTyPE trial utilizes a multidimensional biofeedback system to establish normative mobility profiles in military personnel, laying the groundwork for future precision rehabilitation. Beyond simple monitoring, the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) with continuous wearable sensor data opens new possibilities for precision vestibular rehabilitation. ML models applied to large-scale postural datasets can stratify patients into distinct recovery phenotypes; for instance, analysis of center-of-pressure entropy metrics in post-concussion vestibular dysfunction has identified statistically significant reductions in signal complexity under sensory-conflict conditions, providing data-driven biomarkers to guide individualized intervention strategies. AI-driven digital therapeutics can further translate these insights into closed-loop exercise systems that dynamically modulate task parameters—such as target velocity or amplitude in gaze stabilization tasks—based on real-time performance feedback, rather than fixed dose-escalation protocols. These dynamic systems facilitate individualized, home-based rehabilitation by adjusting to the patient's recovery progress in real-time, reducing dependence on on-site supervision while maintaining therapeutic efficacy, though challenges including long-term patient engagement and digital health literacy warrant continued attention. Smartphone-based tools Recent advancements allow for the remote, quantitative assessment of postural instability in concussion patients using smartphone accelerometers. Studies demonstrate that balance data collected under various surface and visual conditions significantly distinguish concussion patients from healthy controls. Such objective metrics provide practical utility in monitoring recovery trajectories and informing return-to-sport decisions. Emerging adjunctive technologies Complementary therapies using vibrotactile feedback and electrical vestibular stimulation are gaining traction in vestibular rehabilitation. Vibrotactile feedback, often integrated with gamification, addresses the poor compliance associated with repetitive conventional VOR exercises. By integrating simultaneous visual and tactile inputs, these systems enhance multisensory compensation for impaired vestibular function, leading to improved VOR gain even after brief training periods. Limitations and future directions Current research on vestibular rehabilitation technologies faces limitations in establishing robust levels of evidence due to small sample sizes and high study heterogeneity. Consequently, future research must prioritize developing standardized, objective outcome measures and optimal treatment programs tailored to individual patient characteristics and recovery stages. Beyond research limitations, the practical implementation of VRT faces significant systemic barriers in certain healthcare environments, such as South Korea. Domestically, dedicated rehabilitation programs run by specialized physical therapists remain scarce due to structural constraints, including short outpatient consultation times, a lack of standardized therapist training, and insufficient insurance reimbursement for prolonged exercise-based therapies. To overcome both these scientific and structural limitations, future directions should strongly focus on an integrated, hybrid care model. By combining brief, physician-led education in the clinic with the active prescription of digital therapeutics—such as app-based VRT, wearable biofeedback, and remote monitoring—clinicians can effectively bypass temporal and spatial constraints. This technology-assisted, home-based approach provides a realistic pathway to deliver continuous, high-quality, and precise individualized treatment, ultimately maximizing vestibular recovery for patients with persistent post-concussion dizziness within resource-limited clinical environments. CONCLUSION Recently, clinical and research efforts for PCVD have shifted beyond symptomatic management toward “pathophysiology-centered precision rehabilitation.” This approach emphasizes evaluating the complex interactions between peripheral, central, and cervical systems to explain individual symptoms and provide tailored interventions. For effective recovery, individualized VRT programs should be initiated from the early stages, with specialized cervicovestibular programs integrated following a systematic differential diagnosis. Furthermore, the integration of cutting-edge technologies, such as VR and wearable sensors, into multidisciplinary assessment systems allows for more precise, data-driven treatment planning. By transitioning to these personalized and technology-enhanced strategies, clinicians can minimize the risk of long-term sequelae and optimize a successful, functional return to daily life and sports for patients with PCVD.

chunks.content: Nonstandard Abbreviations and Acronyms ARENA Australasian Registry of Screening ECGs in National Athletes ARVC arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy SCD sudden cardiac death TWI T‐wave inversion TWI V2–3 T‐wave inversion in leads V 2 and V 3 Clinical Perspective What Is New? This study found that isolated T‐wave inversion in leads V 2 and V 3 was 4 times as common in female athletes compared with male athletes and nearly 5 times as common in endurance compared with nonendurance athletes. The finding of isolated T‐wave inversion in leads V 2 and V 3 was the most common ECG abnormality in female athletes and was not associated with cardiac pathology or major cardiac events in this large ECG data set in elite athletes. What Are the Clinical Implications? Our data support that isolated TWI V2–3 may be considered a normal ECG finding in asymptomatic female athletes, which would lower the false‐positive rate of ECG screening in female athletes. Cardiac screening of athletes is common internationally, although the exact protocol may vary. , , In Australia and New Zealand, organized programs for cardiac screening of young athletes occur only at the elite level. The Australasian College of Sport and Exercise Physicians position statement recommends preparticipation screening of athletes with a history, physical examination, and 12‐lead ECG on entry to an elite program and then every 2 years until the age of 25 years. “Elite athletes” are those playing in professional competitions, in national or state institutes of sport, and others for whom sports training and competition is their primary activity. Most individual sporting organizations in Australia and New Zealand have a cardiac screening policy; these are largely uniform, commencing at age 15 to 17 years. Female athletes are reported to have a higher proportion of abnormal screening ECGs, , , despite a rate of sudden cardiac death (SCD) that is 4 to 10 times lower than in male athletes. , , , Female athletes have a higher prevalence of T‐wave inversion in leads V 2 and V 3 (TWI V2–3 ) than male athletes, which is often not associated with cardiac pathology. , , , Endurance athletes also are reported to have a higher prevalence of TWI V2–3 than nonendurance athletes. , , TWI V2–3 is considered abnormal for athletes aged ≥16 years in the International Criteria for Athlete ECG Interpretation due to its association with cardiomyopathies, including arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. TWI in leads V 1 , V 2 , and V 3 in individuals aged ≥14 years (in the absence of complete right bundle‐branch block [RBBB]) is a major criterion for diagnosis of the right ventricular phenotype of arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy (ARVC) according to the Marcus criteria and the 2024 European Task Force criteria. This study aimed to determine (1) the prevalence of isolated TWI V2–3 in different sexes and sporting disciplines and (2) whether isolated TWI V2–3 is associated with clinical pathology using a large data set of elite athlete screening ECGs from Australia and New Zealand. Methods Cardiac screening records of elite athletes were obtained from the ARENA (Australasian Registry of ECGs of National Athletes) project and combined with previous athlete cohort studies conducted by the research team in Australia , and New Zealand. Methods for these studies have been previously reported. , , Briefly, retrospective and prospective data were collected from each participating sporting organization and included demographic information, screening ECGs and results, details of any follow‐up testing, diagnoses, and major adverse cardiac outcomes. , , , Retrospective data covered all available records since the commencement of the sporting organization's cardiac screening policy (generally from 2012 to 2015) until the date of collection (2022–2024). Athletes were included if a copy of the ECG from the study period was available and they were aged <40 years at the time of screening. Athletes were screened with personal and family history, physical examination, and resting 12‐lead ECG. Follow‐up testing and evaluation was conducted if required by each sporting organization. ECGs were interpreted at the time they were undertaken by sports physicians, general practitioners, or cardiologists with expertise in athlete ECG interpretation using contemporary athlete‐specific ECG criteria. All ECGs were re‐reviewed by a member of the research team in accordance with the International Criteria for Athlete ECG Interpretation. All abnormal ECGs and all ECGs with contradictory interpretation between the original screening physician and the research team underwent additional review by 2 expert sports cardiologists, and in the event of a disagreement, the majority view was used. Athletes were considered to have an abnormal ECG if they had at least 1 ECG requiring further evaluation (abnormal or with ≥2 borderline findings) according to the International Criteria. Athletes were considered to have an abnormal ECG if they had at least 1 ECG requiring further evaluation (abnormal or with ≥2 borderline findings) according to the International Criteria. If athletes had >1 abnormal ECG, only the first was included in the analyses. Athletes were considered isolated TWI V2–3 cases if they had an abnormal ECG with TWI ≥1 mm in depth in leads V 2 and V 3 and no other abnormal ECG findings according to the International Criteria and were aged ≥16 years (ie, the finding could not be considered a juvenile T‐wave pattern). In accordance with the International Criteria, athletes with a biphasic T wave in V 3 only were considered normal. ECGs of isolated TWI V2–3 cases underwent additional independent review by 2 members of the research team blinded as to sex and sport, with any discrepancies resolved by a third senior clinician reviewer. Endurance sports included middle‐ and long‐distance running, cycling, rowing, canoeing, swimming, triathlon, and cross‐country skiing. Paralympic athletes were listed separately. There was 86% agreement between reviewers on cases for inclusion, with disagreement resolved by a third senior clinician. The finding was most common in female and endurance athletes (Table ). One (male) athlete refused further evaluation, and 1 (male) athlete had not yet completed follow‐up. Isolated TWI V2–3 was the most common abnormal ECG finding in female athletes' screening ECGs (36% of abnormal ECGs in female athletes compared with 13% in male athletes). The second and third most common abnormalities in female athletes were other abnormal TWI and ≥2 premature ventricular contractions. None of the female athletes with isolated TWI V2–3 had other ECG abnormalities on subsequent cardiac screening, and 70% had an earlier or later normal ECG. Two male athletes had later ECGs with other abnormalities (TWI in other leads, pathological Q waves). Overall, female athletes had a higher proportion of abnormal ECGs compared with male athletes (4.2% versus 2.6%, P =0.004; Table , with details of other ECG abnormalities stratified by sex in Table ). If TWI V2–3 was considered a normal finding in female athletes, female and male athletes would have similar proportions of abnormal ECGs (2.6% versus 2.6%, P =0.95). Sporting Discipline Differences All cases of isolated TWI V2–3 were in endurance (Figure [ ]) or mixed sport (Figure [ ]) athletes. Isolated TWI V2–3 was more common in endurance compared with nonendurance athletes, after adjusting for sex (adjusted odds ratio, 4.8 [95% CI, 2.5–9.5]; Table ). Bifid T waves were noted in 61%, deep TWI in 19%, and incomplete RBBB in 31%. The ST segment preceding TWI was either isoelectric (56%) or ascending convex (44%), although more commonly isoelectric in female athletes (67% versus 22%, P =0.02). J‐point elevation was present in 36% of athletes with TWI V2–3 but less common in female athletes compared with males (26% versus 67%, P =0.03). Voltage criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy and right ventricular hypertrophy was uncommon in female athletes with TWI V2–3 but was present in the majority of male athletes (left ventricular hypertrophy: 4% versus 78%, P <0.0001; right ventricular hypertrophy: 7% versus 78%, P <0.0001; Table ). Isolated TWI V2–3 was the most common abnormal finding in female athletes' screening ECGs and almost entirely accounted for the higher proportion of female athletes with an abnormal ECG compared with male athletes. Female Athletes Our results showing female athletes have a higher proportion of abnormal screening ECGs are consistent with previous studies using the International Criteria. , , Generally, the findings in these studies have not been matched by a higher number of diagnoses associated with SCD. A study comparing 162 patients with ARVC against 129 healthy young controls with anterior TWI found that 81% of patients with ARVC had an abnormal ECG and anterior TWI was the most common ECG abnormality (51%). Consistent with our report, other recent studies presenting cardiac screening results do not include any examples of female athletes with isolated TWI V2–3 being diagnosed with ARVC. , , , , Our study found that female sex was strongly and independently associated with increased odds of isolated TWI V2–3 , adjusting for sporting discipline. Some smaller studies report a higher proportion (5%–8%) , , , of female athletes with TWI V2–3 , compared with 1.5% in our study. This difference may be the result of chance/natural variation in smaller sample sizes (n<1000). Malhotra et al found a higher proportion of TWI V2–3 in female compared with male athletes (2.1% versus 0.3%, P <0.0001), none of whom were diagnosed with ARVC after extensive investigation. Conversely, a large UK cohort of 11 168 male football (soccer) players screened at the age of 16 years reported diagnoses of ARVC in 2 male athletes: one had isolated TWI V2–3 on ECG (together with symptoms of palpitations/dizziness), and the other had a normal ECG and history and physical examination but an abnormal echocardiogram. In addition, an audit of cardiac screening in UK cricket reported 1 diagnosis of ARVC in a male player, who had isolated TWI V2–3 and a normal history and physical examination. As in previous studies, we found that the ST segment preceding TWI was more commonly isoelectric (than not) in female compared with male athletes with isolated TWI V2–3 (67% versus 22%, P =0.02). , We also found that J‐point elevation was less common in female athletes with TWI V2–3 compared with male athletes (26% versus 67%, P =0.03). Thus, our results are consistent with the findings of Malhotra et al, who suggest that a J point and ST segment in line with the onset of the QRS complex may be potential markers of disease in male athletes with anterior TWI but not in female athletes. Finocchiaro et al aimed to differentiate between benign TWI and ARVC and concluded that a J point <0.1 mV preceding anterior TWI was not a useful way to differentiate physiology from pathology. They found that a J point <0.1 mV was common in those with ARVC and in the group of healthy young people (including athletes) with anterior TWI. However, consideration of the J point and ST segment is included in the 2024 European Task Force criteria, which classifies TWI in the right precordial leads in the absence of complete RBBB and not preceded by J‐point/ST‐segment elevation , as a major criterion for ARVC diagnosis. This could be due to differences in conditioning if this is a physiological adaptation or differences in lead placement. Lead placement and breast tissue have been suggested as possible explanations for sex differences in isolated TWI V2–3 . , , , The prevalence of anterior TWI in prepubertal children has been shown to be similar in boys and girls, which supports the theory that breast tissue in older female athletes could affect lead placement. This study compared 68 endurance athletes with 41 controls and measured cardiac displacement and orientation within the thorax using horizontal long‐axis images. Smaller thoracic size was found to contribute, which could be a factor in female athletes. Our data provide supportive electrocardiographic evidence of this phenomenon. Specifically, more than two thirds of athletes in this cohort with TWI V2–3 demonstrated a negative net QRS vector in V 3 . This finding among healthy athletes is likely explained by anatomic counterclockwise rotation of the heart due to right ventricular–predominant exercise‐induced dilation. While future work examining the relationship between net QRS vector and TWI inversion patterns is warranted, this pattern may serve as an additional ECG finding to supporting the benign nature of TWI V2–3 among endurance athletes. Female athletes are underrepresented in sports cardiology research, including data from preparticipation screening programs. , In addition, this data set is composed of elite athletes at a high competitive level. The vast majority were tier 3 (highly trained/national level), tier 4 (elite/international level), or tier 5 (world class). Athletes at these higher levels generally train more and at higher intensity, which may be relevant to the degree of cardiac remodeling evident on their screening ECGs (especially for endurance athletes). This was a real‐world study with a number of limitations. First, data were limited to the records available at participating sporting organizations, and most were collected retrospectively. It is possible that these records were incomplete and that some athlete screening ECGs and follow‐up tests were performed but not included. However, we used our best endeavors to work with sports medicine staff at participating organizations to identify all relevant records, particularly for athletes requiring further evaluation. In 2022, approximately 2.3 million children and adolescents (3.2%) in the United States were diagnosed with a concussion or brain injury, with prevalence increasing with age: from 1.0% in children aged 0–5 years, to 2.3% in those 6–11 years, and 5.9% in adolescents aged 12–17 years ( ). National surveys report lifetime concussion/head injury estimates in youth ranging from 2.5 to 18.3%, with the highest prevalence found in adolescents aged 13–17 years ( ). Annually, over 120,000 emergency department visits occur in children under 18 due to mTBI, particularly in males ( ). Approximately 87% of pediatric TBIs recorded in national trauma databases are classified as mild, and most children recover within a few weeks ( ). However, a subset of children experience prolonged symptoms, hospitalization, or complications—demonstrating that even mild TBIs can lead to an extended recovery depending on injury severity, risk factors, and mechanism of injury ( ). After concussion, many children and adolescents experience a range of symptoms across physical, cognitive, emotional, and sleep related systems ( ). Given that processing of visual information is supported by extensive cortical circuitry, the visual system is particularly vulnerable post-concussion, making visual symptoms highly prevalent ( ; ). Commonly reported symptoms include double vision, blurred vision, headaches during near work, light sensitivity, and difficulty reading or focusing ( ; ; ; ). Studies consistently show that convergence insufficiency (CI) and accommodative dysfunction are among the most common diagnoses post-concussion ( ; ; ). Convergence insufficiency is a binocular vision-related disorder in which the eyes do not work together effectively during near tasks, resulting in difficulty maintaining alignment and fusion ( ). Accommodative dysfunction is characterized by an impaired ability to focus and/or sustain focus during near visual activities ( ; ). In our recent study, we reported that these vision-related dysfunctions may persist for months post-injury and are associated with prolonged recovery and reduced quality of life ( ). Frequency of vergence or accommodative dysfunction in both the subacute (15 days–12 weeks) and chronic (>12 weeks–1 year) phases from the time since concussion were similar, indicating that such deficits may not resolve spontaneously and could benefit from evaluation by a specialized eye care provider ( ). The Convergence Insufficiency Symptom Survey (CISS) is a 15-item questionnaire developed to assess symptoms in patients with CI ( ). While initially designed and validated to diagnose symptomatic CI and used as an outcome measure in large clinical treatment trials like the CITT and CITT-Attention and Reading Trial ( ; , ; ), the CISS has since been adapted for use in concussion populations to capture symptom burden ( ) when doing near activities. The CITT established the clinical utility of the CISS in children aged 9–17 years, demonstrating the effectiveness of vergence/accommodative therapy in reducing symptoms ( ) in symptomatic children with CI. Standard concussion scales such as the Post-Concussion Symptom Scale (PCSS) only assess whether a patient declares they have “Sensitivity to Light,” or have “vision problems” which does not capture the variety of vision-related symptoms that may present following concussion ( ). Although not a diagnostic tool for identifying CI following concussion, the CISS helps clinicians identify symptomatic individuals who may benefit from a comprehensive visual function assessment ( ; ). Our earlier retrospective study has shown that the CISS is sensitive to the broader symptomatology associated with post-concussion vergence and/or accommodation deficits and may offer a cost-effective, accessible tool for tracking symptoms outside of eye care clinics ( ). Additionally, studies suggest that dividing the CISS into subscores itemized into different domains such as somatic (e.g., headaches, eye strain), performance (e.g., re-reading lines, poor concentration), and vision-related (e.g., double vision, blurring) can help characterize symptom profiles following naturally occurring CI ( ), dyslexia ( ), and concussion ( ). Using the CISS, we have demonstrated that individuals who have experienced a concussion report significantly higher somatic-related subscores in comparison to visually normal controls. Additionally, our research indicates that vergence and/or accommodation deficits following a concussion were associated with higher total CISS scores and vision-related subscores in a pediatric and adolescent cohort ( ). In this paper, we present a prospective study designed to compare vergence and/or accommodation deficits and symptom burden in children and adolescents with and without a history of concussion using the CISS. Our objectives are twofold: first, to evaluate total CISS scores and subscores across somatic-, performance-, and vision-related subscores between concussed and non-concussed participants; and second, to determine whether symptom severity as measured by the CISS differs between concussed individuals with and without identified vergence and/or accommodation deficits. We hypothesized that concussed participants would report significantly greater overall symptom burden than non-concussed controls, and within the concussion group, those with vergence and/or accommodation deficits would exhibit higher CISS subscores, particularly in vision-related subscores. Methods Institutional review board approval This study received approval from the Institutional Review Boards of Boston Children’s Hospital (Boston, Massachusetts, United States), Stanford University (Stanford, California, United States), and Salus University (Elkins Park, Pennsylvania, United States). Written informed consent was obtained from a parent or legal guardian of each participant, and written assent was obtained from all participants prior to enrolment in the study. Participant recruitment and eligibility Participants were recruited from Boston Children’s Hospital, Stanford University, and the Pennsylvania College of Optometry at Salus University. Control participants were enrolled through word-of-mouth referrals, departmental staff, local community, and patients attending routine eye examinations at the affiliated clinics. Participants with concussion were recruited from dedicated concussion clinics at Boston Children’s Hospital and Stanford University or were referred to the vision care practices of the senior investigators (TLR and AR) for post-concussion assessment. These referrals were made for individuals experiencing persistent post-concussion symptoms, regardless of vision-specific complaints. The inclusion criteria for the concussion group required a physician-diagnosed concussion in accordance with the Berlin Consensus Statement on Concussion in Sport, with the study visit occurring 4 weeks to 12 months post-injury. Control participants were eligible if they had no history of concussion and no known accommodative or vergence deficits. All participants were aged between 8 and <18 years, demonstrated best-corrected distance visual acuity of 20/25 or better in each eye, and wore appropriate refractive correction. Detailed inclusion and exclusion criteria are provided in and . Symptom assessments Convergence insufficiency symptom survey The CISS is a 15-item questionnaire ( ) validated for use in patients with CI ( ). Each item is rated on a Likert scale ranging from “never” (0) to “always” (4), yielding a total score between 0 and 60, with higher scores indicating greater symptom severity. The CISS items were further divided into subcategories: 7 somatic-related symptoms (CISS-S), 5 performance-related symptoms (CISS-P), and 3 vision-related symptoms (CISS-V) ( ; ; ). CISS subscores were normalized by dividing the category’s total response score by the number of items in the category to control for each subscore containing different numbers of items ( ). Vision and visual function assessment Following the administration of the CISS, each participant underwent a comprehensive visual function examination conducted by a pediatric optometrist, including assessment of distance and near visual acuity, stereopsis, ocular motility, ocular alignment, vergence, and accommodation. Ocular alignment was evaluated using the cover-uncover test, with deviation magnitude measured by the prism and alternate cover test. The vergence assessment included near-point of convergence (NPC), near vergence facility, and fusional amplitudes for near convergence and divergence. Accommodation was evaluated using amplitude of accommodation (AA) and monocular accommodative facility. Any examiner- or participant-noted difficulties with base-out (convergence demand) or base-in (divergence demand) prisms during vergence facility testing were noted. Similarly, difficulties with minus (increased demand) or plus (decreased demand) lenses during accommodative facility testing were noted. Diagnoses related to vergence and accommodation were made based on visual function testing results and criteria described in ( ; ; ). Further details of the examination procedures can be found in . Since a Shapiro–Wilk test indicated non-normality for CISS scores, non-parametric Mann–Whitney U tests were conducted to compare total CISS scores as well as subscores between concussed and control participants. Separately for the control and concussed groups, Friedman tests were used to compare normalized subscores within each group. A two-sided alpha-value of 0.05 was set as the threshold for statistical significance in all analyses. Wilcoxon signed rank post-hoc tests were used for any pairwise comparisons between normalized subscores within each group, with an adjusted alpha-value of 0.017. Finally, Mann Whitney U tests were conducted to compare total CISS scores and subscores between concussed participants with and without vergence and/or accommodative deficits. However, no significant difference was observed between CISS-P (0.20 [0.0 to 0.60]) and CISS-S (0.29 [0.00 to 0.43]; z = −1.24, p = 0.215) subscores. Twenty one (80.8%) had both vergence and accommodation deficits; 5 (19.2%) had only accommodation deficits; none of the participants had only vergence deficits ( ; , ). The median total CISS scores were significantly higher in the concussed group with vergence and/or accommodation deficits (31.50 [22.25 to 38.75]) compared to concussed participants without deficits (19.50 [15.75 to 21.25]; U = 47, p = 0.022; ). Compared with participants without vergence and/or accommodation deficits, those with deficits also had significantly higher normalized median subscores for CISS-V (concussed with deficits: 1.33 [0.75 to 2.25], concussed without deficits: 0.50 [0.00 to 0.67]; U = 35, p < 0.01) and for CISS-P (concussed with deficits: 2.40 [2.05 to 3.20], concussed without deficits: 1.50 [1.15 to 2.10]; U = 54.5; p = 0.047). No significant group difference was observed for CISS-S (concussed with deficits: 2.14 [1.61 to 2.82], concussed without deficits 1.43 [0.82 to 1.75]; U = 61, p = 0.084; ). Symptom severity in control and concussed groups Symptom severity across the 15 CISS items revealed distinct differences in symptom reporting trends between control and concussed participants. In the control group, symptom severity was generally low, with most symptoms

No significant group difference was observed for CISS-S (concussed with deficits: 2.14 [1.61 to 2.82], concussed without deficits 1.43 [0.82 to 1.75]; U = 61, p = 0.084; ). Symptom severity in control and concussed groups Symptom severity across the 15 CISS items revealed distinct differences in symptom reporting trends between control and concussed participants. In the control group, symptom severity was generally low, with most symptoms receiving a mean score close to zero. The top five reported symptoms in this group were “Lose Place,” “Sleepy,” “Lose Concentration, “Re-Read,” and “Tired Eyes,” with mean symptom scores ranging from 0.2 to 0.75. CISS-V items such as “Double Vision” and “Words Blur” were among the least reported in this group, with mean scores closer to zero ( ). In contrast, the concussed group demonstrated a greater symptom burden across all categories. The distribution of symptom burden was similar between those with vergence and/or accommodation deficits and those without, with only slight differences in magnitude; therefore, these subgroups were combined and analyzed as a single concussed group. The most frequently reported symptoms were “Headaches,” “Lose Concentration,” “Tired Eyes,” “Re-Read,” and “Lose Place,” with mean symptom scores ranging from 0.6 to 2.8. Headaches had the highest mean symptom severity score. CISS-V items, such as “Words Blur” and “Double Vision,” were reported more frequently in the concussed group, particularly among participants with vergence and/or accommodation deficits, compared to controls ( ). Discussion Concussed participants reported significantly higher total CISS scores than visually normal controls with no history of concussion, along with higher scores on somatic, performance, and vision-related subscores. Within the concussed cohort, those with vergence and/or accommodative deficits experienced greater symptom severity across all CISS subscores, particularly for CISS-V and CISS-P, compared to concussed participants without such deficits. Accommodative and vergence deficits were common in our concussed cohort, consistent with previous studies ( ; ; ). Symptom reporting can vary depending on how visual complaints are perceived or described by patients; for example, visual discomfort might manifest as general fatigue, headaches, losing concentration, or reading difficulties, which can fall under general somatic- or cognitive-related symptoms without specifically recognized as stemming from visual function problems ( ; ). This emphasizes using the CISS to characterize symptoms following concussion and using the subscores to further help understand the presence of vergence and/or accommodation deficits or symptom provocation when doing near work ( ; ). The CISS can help identify symptom patterns and guide referral decisions even when overt vision symptoms are not the primary complaint ( ; ). Interestingly, both concussed and control groups demonstrated the highest symptom burden in CISS-P items, although the magnitude was significantly greater in the concussed group. This trend mirrors findings in patients with naturally occurring CI. In the CITT randomized clinical trial, performance-related symptoms were more frequently endorsed than eye-related symptoms among children with symptomatic naturally occurring CI ( ; ). In our study, the similar CISS-P and CISS-S scores, combined with elevated CISS-V scores in the concussed group, suggest a broader neurological disruption affecting multiple systems, rather than just vision-related dysfunction. CISS-S in our concussed cohort were reported with similar frequency as CISS-P subscores. This pronounced somatic symptom burden may reflect underlying discomfort when facing visually demanding tasks. Notably, even in the absence of measurable vergence or accommodation deficits, elevated somatic and performance symptom reporting may suggest subjective experience of discomfort and difficulty with visual system use. Therefore, patients with normal vergence and accommodation findings who report high somatic and performance symptoms might still experience ongoing subjective discomfort and strain. Rehabilitation strategies focused on alleviating symptoms even when clinical findings are normal could effectively manage persistent post-concussion symptoms. These findings underscore the importance of systematically evaluating visual function in concussed patients, as addressing visual function related deficits can inform targeted interventions to help reduce symptom burden and facilitate recovery ( ; ). The distribution of symptoms across subscores in concussed patients may indicate disruption in the neural systems beyond the oculomotor circuit. The visual system recruits an extensive cortical network, and post-concussive vulnerability may extend to those networks that also support visual attention, memory, and visual-motor coordination ( ; ). These mechanisms might explain somatic symptoms such as headaches or tired eyes during reading or close work, even in the absence of measurable vergence deficits. A large proportion of our concussed participants were in the chronic phase of recovery (median time since injury: 107 days), yet symptom burden remained high. This supports previous findings that while vergence and accommodative deficits may persist months post-injury, symptom intensity can also remain high regardless of time since injury (

These mechanisms might explain somatic symptoms such as headaches or tired eyes during reading or close work, even in the absence of measurable vergence deficits. A large proportion of our concussed participants were in the chronic phase of recovery (median time since injury: 107 days), yet symptom burden remained high. This supports previous findings that while vergence and accommodative deficits may persist months post-injury, symptom intensity can also remain high regardless of time since injury ( ; ; ). Furthermore, the high prevalence of multiple concussions in our sample (48.4% with more than one concussion) may also contribute to greater symptom severity and complexity, as cumulative injuries have been associated with prolonged recovery and increased risk of vergence and/or accommodation deficits ( ). Studies suggest that persistent vergence and/or accommodation deficits post-concussion often require intervention and do not resolve spontaneously, reinforcing the need for early identification and monitoring ( ). This study reinforces the utility of the CISS in identifying patients with potential vision-related deficits following concussion. Notably, when the CISS-V subscores are flagged as concerning, they can help pinpoint children and adolescents with vergence and/or accommodation deficits. This correlation was observed in our retrospective study ( ) and was corroborated with this prospective study. Although not a diagnostic tool, the CISS can identify individuals with pronounced symptoms who may benefit from comprehensive visual function assessment and, when appropriate, vision rehabilitation ( ; ; ; ; ). Prior research indicated that patients with post-concussion convergence and accommodative insufficiencies have a favorable response to vision rehabilitation, with 85% achieving either symptom resolution or improvement ( ). However, a recent scoping review highlights a critical need for high-quality randomized clinical trials to thoroughly evaluate the effectiveness of vison rehabilitation intervention following concussion ( ; ). This study has several limitations. First, the number of concussed participants without vergence and accommodation deficits was relatively low, limiting subgroup comparisons and necessitating a larger sample size to confirm the replicability of these findings. Second, the characterization of mTBI may have been heterogenous, as mechanisms of injury and impact characteristics varied across participants. The modest sample size also limited our ability to include age, sex, prior concussion history and time since injury as covariates in the statistical analysis. Finally, although the CISS was administered uniformly across sites, variations in verbal versus written administration could potentially affect how patients rate symptom frequency, as previously reported in studies comparing clinician- and self-administered versions of the CISS ( ; ). Conclusion Adolescents with a history of concussion report significantly higher overall symptom burden on the Convergence Insufficiency Symptom Survey (CISS) compared with visually-normal controls. Higher vision-related and performance-related subscores were associated with the presence of vergence and accommodation deficits, while elevated somatic and performance subscores may reflect increased subjective discomfort and difficulty during visually demanding near tasks such as reading. Concurrent assessment of vergence and accommodation function alongside CISS scores may help identify individuals most likely to benefit from vision rehabilitation aimed at improving vergence and accommodation function and reducing somatic and performance-related symptoms during cognitively demanding near tasks.

chunks.content: SARS-CoV-2, the novel coronavirus that causes COVID-19 illness, presents unique health issues that should be considered in student-athletes prior to a return to sports and exercise. While the vast majority of young persons afflicted with the coronavirus have mild symptoms or remain asymptomatic, the infection can cause direct injury or inflammation to the heart and lungs, especially in patients ill enough to require hospitalization. Cardiopulmonary concerns from COVID-19 arise from data in severely ill adult patients, where approximately 1 in 5 hospitalized patients suffers from cardiac or thromboembolic (clotting) complications. , However, evidence on the prevalence and risks of these complications in adolescents and in individuals who have had a milder form of the illness remains limited. An expert task force was formed from the National Federation of State High School Associations (NFHS) and the American Medical Society for Sports Medicine (AMSSM) to provide guidance for the medical assessment of student-athletes with prior COVID-19 illness before sports participation. The task force recommends that schools consider a supplemental questionnaire addressing medical issues specific to COVID-19 ( ). Any positive response from the survey should trigger an evaluation by a medical provider prior to sports participation. Prior COVID-19 Illness Confirmed diagnosis: Every student-athlete with a prior confirmed diagnosis (positive test) for COVID-19 should undergo an evaluation by one’s medical provider prior to sports participation ( ). Ongoing symptoms related to COVID-19 should be explored, including the presence of chest pain or shortness of breath with exertion, palpitations (heart racing), excessive fatigue, or decreased exercise tolerance. Written medical clearance is recommended prior to participation in sports. Mild to moderate illness: Student-athletes who had mild to moderate symptoms from COVID-19 that were managed at home should be seen by their medical provider for a detailed history of persisting symptoms or changes in their health status that may necessitate further testing or evaluation by a specialist. An electrocardiogram (ECG) may be considered prior to sports participation dependent on clinical suspicion for myocarditis (heart infection) and cardiology resources and expertise for ECG interpretation in young athletes. , , Severe (hospitalized) illness: Student-athletes who were hospitalized with severe illness from COVID-19, including multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children, have a higher risk for heart or lung complications such as arrhythmias, myocarditis, heart failure, sudden cardiac arrest (SCA), and pulmonary embolism (blood clots to the lungs). A comprehensive cardiac evaluation is recommended in consultation with a cardiology specialist, which may include any or all of the following (as clinically indicated): ECG, cardiac biomarkers such as high-sensitivity troponin, echocardiogram, cardiac magnetic resonance imaging, Holter monitor, or stress test. , , Follow-up pulmonary evaluation and testing may also be indicated, including chest radiograph, spirometry, functional testing to assess bronchospasm or oxygen desaturation with exercise, chest computed tomography scan, or additional pulmonology consultation. Ongoing symptoms: Student-athletes with ongoing symptoms from diagnosed COVID-19 illness require a comprehensive evaluation to exclude heart and lung disorders that carry a risk of arrhythmia, respiratory compromise, SCA, or sudden death. Specifically, myocarditis may present with ongoing symptoms of chest pain, palpitations, shortness of breath, or exercise intolerance. , Ongoing symptoms from COVID-19 may also indicate pulmonary issues such as acquired or worsening asthma, pneumonia, or pulmonary embolism that may cause chest pain, shortness of breath, tachycardia (fast heart rate), or a low oxygen saturation. The diagnosis of myocarditis, pulmonary embolism, or any other cardiopulmonary disorder should be managed per current medical guidelines. The student-athlete should not return to sports and/or exercise until medically cleared by a physician. , Other considerations: Evaluation by a medical provider should also be considered for the following circumstances: Any “close contact” (ie, family or household member) with confirmed COVID-19 infection Student-athletes with underlying medical conditions that place them at higher risk of severe COVID-19 illness, such as uncontrolled or moderate to severe asthma, a serious heart condition, obesity, diabetes, chronic kidney or liver disease, or a weakened immune system Student-athletes with prior symptoms suggestive of (but not confirmed) COVID-19, especially if symptoms were severe or required hospitalization New COVID-19 Infections Schools should consider a daily tracking tool to confirm student-athletes are appropriately self-monitoring and have not developed symptoms of COVID-19. In addition, it is suggested that schools establish a COVID-19 response team to help develop and implement policies and procedures for a safe return to sport in their school and to assist in COVID-19 symptom screening, reporting, and contact tracing. Student-athletes should not attend school, sports practices, or competitions if feeling ill and should be referred to their medical provider for possible COVID-19 testing if they present with any of the following symptoms: fever, new cough, difficulty breathing, shaking chills, chest pain, gastrointestinal symptoms (nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea), loss of taste or smell, sore throat, or an unusual rash or painful discoloration of fingers or toes. Student-athletes who test positive for COVID-19

to help develop and implement policies and procedures for a safe return to sport in their school and to assist in COVID-19 symptom screening, reporting, and contact tracing. Student-athletes should not attend school, sports practices, or competitions if feeling ill and should be referred to their medical provider for possible COVID-19 testing if they present with any of the following symptoms: fever, new cough, difficulty breathing, shaking chills, chest pain, gastrointestinal symptoms (nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea), loss of taste or smell, sore throat, or an unusual rash or painful discoloration of fingers or toes. Student-athletes who test positive for COVID-19 with or without symptoms should be isolated per public health guidelines. No exercise is recommended for at least 14 days from diagnosis and 7 days after all symptoms have resolved. After symptom resolution and prior to sports participation, student-athletes should be evaluated by a medical provider to assess for residual symptoms and the need for additional testing. Written medical clearance prior to sports participation is recommended. Emergency Action Plan Every school is reminded to have a well-rehearsed emergency action plan (EAP) for every sport at every venue to facilitate a coordinated and efficient response to SCA. , , Every school should maintain an on-site automated external defibrillator (AED) program that allows retrieval and use of an AED within 3 minutes of collapse at school athletic venues and buildings. Potential first responders to SCA, including coaches, are encouraged to be trained in cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), the recognition of SCA, and use of an AED. Each school should conduct and document an annual EAP practice drill for SCA among anticipated first responders (ie, athletic trainers, school nurses, coaches, and administrators). AED devices should be maintained according to manufacturer guidelines, including monthly readiness checks and scheduled battery or lead replacement.

chunks.content: WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN? Evidence-based sports injury prevention interventions for athletes often do not transition into routine practice within communities and require deliberate dissemination and implementation (D&I) strategies to bridge the gap and ensure accessibility. Female/woman/girl athletes have unique injury profiles and sporting environments that may require tailored strategies to deliver injury prevention interventions. WHAT ARE THE NEW FINDINGS? Adoption and cumulative use, the most reported D&I outcomes, were generally moderate to high. Positive perceptions, attitudes, intentions, and self-efficacy among athletes and coaches, prior injury experience and higher competition levels were facilitators of D&I in injury prevention programmes for female/woman/girl athletes. Many studies acknowledged health, performance, and environmental factors that could influence female/women/girls’ capability, opportunity and/or motivation to access, participate in, and benefit from evidence-based injury prevention interventions. For female/woman/girl athletes, interventions that are adaptable, sport-specific, engaging, and supported by education and/or workshops and/or policies are most likely to be used. In-person or online pre-season education followed by routine supervision in-season is resource-intensive and may improve implementation; however, further D&I focused studies are required. The whole sport system (eg, athletes, parents, coaches, teachers, health/exercise/medical professionals, trainers and sport administrators) is critical to enhance implementation and sustainability of injury prevention interventions. Introduction Sport injury profiles and rates often differ by sex/gender, and injury outcomes (eg, return to sport and ongoing symptoms) are often worse in female, woman and/or girl (female/women/girl) athletes. Biological differences may partly drive these disparities, so too the interaction of sex/gender and sport context. Female/woman/girl athletes may have different training histories, sport exposure or facilitators and barriers to participation than male/man/boy athletes, ultimately influencing their injury risk. The extent to which injury prevention strategies are implemented with female/woman/girl athletes by athletes, coaches and organisations outside of randomised controlled trials (RCTs) is unclear. Tailoring strategies to female/woman/girl athletes based on injury profile and sport context may be the key to preventing more injuries. Evidence-based interventions often do not inform routine practice in the communities they are meant to benefit, requiring deliberate strategies to expedite the process. Dissemination is the ‘active approach of spreading evidence-based interventions to the target audience via determined channels using planned strategies.’ Implementation encompasses ‘strategies and factors that support the initial integration and use of evidence-based interventions within a specific context’ and sustained use over time. Understanding what effective dissemination and implementation (D&I) strategies exist and factors associated with intervention use across socio-ecological levels will guide practice for athletes, support personnel (eg, coaches and health professionals) and organisations. This scoping review aimed to synthesise evidence related to D&I of injury prevention interventions to inform practical and research recommendations, as part of the Female, Woman and Girl Athlete Injury Prevention (FAIR) Consensus. Five other FAIR Consensus systematic reviews examined the efficacy and/or effectiveness of injury prevention interventions for lower-extremity, upper extremity, spine/trunk/pelvis and concussion injuries in female/woman/girl athletes. In this scoping review, we (1) describe how D&I of injury prevention interventions were measured, (2) examine the level of D&I and factors associated with D&I at multiple socio-ecological levels and (3) explore available D&I strategies. Methods The protocol was based on the Johanna Briggs Institute scoping review best practice guidelines and was registered prospectively on 23 July 2023 ( https://osf.io/eskz7/ ). Reporting was guided by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) extension for Scoping Reviews Checklist ( ). Protocol deviations The protocol was updated (June 2024) to include papers with ≥25% female/woman/girl athletes (previously ≥1 athlete) to better represent the environment for this population. Further, papers only had to include a D&I outcome (protocol stated had to also report factors associated with D&I outcomes; ). Box 1 Equity, diversity and inclusion statement Female, woman and girl: In this review, we refer to the participants as ‘female, woman, and/or girl’ athletes (shortened into female/woman/girl) and ‘male, man, and/or boy’ athletes (male/man/boy). We recognise that these terms are not synonymous and may mean different things to different people. We also use the term ‘gender and/or sex’ (gender/sex). We acknowledge the active conversation on the meaning and definitions of gender and sex and note that the term ‘female(s)’ is not intended to reduce humans to their biological sex, and terms ‘women’ and ‘girls’ are not intended to reduce humans to their gender. Review planning and design: The FAIR Consensus Steering Committee planned and designed this review. This group (n=24, 80% women; n=17, 71% affiliated with IOC Research Centres for the prevention of injury and protection of athlete health) includes academics and sports medicine/health professionals (n=19; 79%) with broad expertise, such as epidemiology (n=18; 75%), injury prevention (n=21; 88%), sport sciences (n=4; 17%), health promotion (n=2; 8%) and career stage (n=7, late career; n=9, mid-career; n=8, early career) from four continents, who are mostly white, and from well-resourced countries.
