This group (n=24, 80% women; n=17, 71% affiliated with IOC Research Centres for the prevention of injury and protection of athlete health) includes academics and sports medicine/health professionals (n=19; 79%) with broad expertise, such as epidemiology (n=18; 75%), injury prevention (n=21; 88%), sport sciences (n=4; 17%), health promotion (n=2; 8%) and career stage (n=7, late career; n=9, mid-career; n=8, early career) from four continents, who are mostly white, and from well-resourced countries. Authors: for this scoping review were chosen by the FAIR Steering Committee based on relevant and diverse experiences, backgrounds, expertise and professions. This research team (n=29, 76% women) consists of early (49%), mid-career (34%) and senior (17%) researchers from physiotherapy, sport and exercise science, nursing, coaching, public health and data science disciplines. Authors are mostly white (83%), with 7% black (African)/African American (n=2), and 10% Asian (n=3). Authors spanned five continents (current residence) with 14% from countries with middle- to low-income birth rates. Authors self-reported lived experience as an athlete (n=13; 45%), coach (n=12; 41%), referee (n=1; 3%), health, medical or exercise practitioner (n=21; 72%) and member of sport organisation (n=12; 41%), government (n=3; 10%) or healthcare committees (n=4; 14%), covering paediatric (n=25; 86%), adult (n= 25; 86%) and Para sport (n=14; 48%) settings. Study participants: These included athletes (49% female/woman/girl), coaches, parents, teachers, athletic trainers, health and exercise professionals and local, national and international sport system administrators. Studies were conducted in 31 countries, across 81 sports. The effects of sociodemographic factors, including sex/gender, were explored. Patient and public involvement The FAIR Consensus External Advisory Committee (EAC) consists of eight women with lived experiences as athletes, team physicians/physiotherapists, coaches, sport scientists and leadership in sport, government, industry and/or healthcare organisations. The EAC provided feedback on this review (eg, eligible sports/populations, interpretation and practical implications) and will contribute to knowledge translation activities. EAC activities are further detailed in the methods of the FAIR consensus statement paper. Eligibility Population . The population of interest included female/woman/girl athletes of any age who were participating in sports competition and/or performance (ie, dance/performing arts) at any level (professional, amateur, grassroots and Para sports). Recreational activity (eg, running/skiing without competition) and active transportation (eg, cycling to work) were excluded. Given the underrepresentation of female/woman/girl athletes in sports medicine research, papers on mixed sex and gender were included, where≥25% were female/woman/girl athletes or individuals (eg, coaches and trainers) who worked with ≥25% of female/woman/girl athletes. The 25% cut-off aimed to increase the likelihood that the D&I strategies considered female/woman/girl athletes. Outcomes : Any D&I outcomes associated with a primary sports injury prevention intervention (eg, musculoskeletal, concussion, central/peripheral nervous system, eye and dental) were included. We considered all D&I terms (eg, awareness, adoption and exercise fidelity) and known implementation and socio-behavioural models/frameworks. Outcomes related to general injury knowledge without explicitly addressing prevention (eg, concussion symptom recognition) were excluded. Intervention: All injury prevention interventions/behaviours were eligible. Secondary prevention interventions were considered if the primary objective was to reduce the risk of subsequent injury. Interventions solely targeting injury risk factors (eg, strength and biomechanics) were excluded. Exposures (Aim 2). Papers evaluating factors associated with D&I of an injury prevention intervention were identified using a combination of D&I determinant models. Factors could be related to any level of the socio-ecological model: individual (eg, athlete injury experience and beliefs) interpersonal (eg, coach gender, relationships with teammates and parent beliefs), sport–system and community (eg, local, national, regional or international sporting body or government mandates/guidelines) or society (eg, public opinion/norms). Factors could also relate to intervention (eg, intervention duration and delivery method) or sociodemographic factors (eg, region and socioeconomic status). Study design . All primary research designs were included, from peer-reviewed journals or thesis/dissertation chapters. Review articles, protocols, conference abstracts and editorials/commentaries were excluded. Information sources An expert evidence synthesis health sciences librarian (KAH) developed and executed the search strategy according to the Cochrane Handbook and PERSiST guidance (implementing Prisma in Exercise, Rehabilitation, Sport medicine and Sports science), in consultation with authors KC, CE, CM, OO, BP and EV ( ). The search consisted of three main concepts: sports, prevention (both adapted from the sixth Consensus on Concussion in Sports) and dissemination/implementation. Nine databases were searched from 1996 to 2023 (Medline-OVID, CINAHL-EBSCOhost, APA PsycINFO-OVID, Cochrane Systematic Review Database-OVID, CENTRAL-OVID, SPORTDiscus-EBSCOhost, EMBASE-OVID and ERIC-EBSCOhost). ProQuest Dissertation & Theses Global was searched for dissertation/theses. Databases were searched on 14 December 2023, except CENTRAL and Cochrane Systematic Review Database (19 December 2023). Records were exported to Covidence (Version 2, Veritas Health Innovation, Melbourne, Australia) for deduplication and screening. Selection of sources A rapid screen by eight reviewers excluded irrelevant (not related to sports) records and animal research. Inter-rater agreement was then established among all reviewers on a sample set of 50 records, with a minimum threshold of 80%. Reviewers not meeting this threshold screened another 50 records, continuing until ≥80% agreement was achieved. Twenty-four reviewers working in blinded pairs then screened titles/abstracts and full texts. Disagreements within pairs during screening and data extraction were resolved by consensus or discussion with a third reviewer. Quality assessment The Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT) 2018 was used to assess methodological quality across different study designs (quantitative RCTs, quantitative non-randomised trials, quantitative descriptive, qualitative and mixed methods). The MMAT was amended to remove the adherence/compliance criterion (as this was an inclusion criterion for the review). Scores were presented using a percentage descriptor, from 0 (no criteria met) to 100% (all criteria met). Based on the total score, individual papers were classified as high (≥75%), moderate (26%–74%) or low (≤25%) quality ( ). Data charting and appraisal A data extraction spreadsheet and instructions were developed and updated iteratively (by BP, CM and OO; ) during data extraction on a subset of eight papers. Following training (by BP, CM and OO), 24 authors in blinded pairs concurrently extracted data, including study characteristics (eg, design, year and country), participant details (eg, sport, role, age and competition level), intervention details (eg, type and duration), D&I outcomes (eg, 80% aware of mouthguards), D&I exposure variables (eg, delivery method and sport setting) and MMAT scores. Data extracted from qualitative papers were themes and exemplar quotes related to D&I outcomes and/or exposure variables of interest. Synthesis By population . Papers (n, %) were categorised according to participant type/s (by socio-ecological levels), sport/s represented, competition level/s, athlete age-group/s and injury prevention intervention type ( ). Box 2 Definitions of participant and intervention type, competition level, age-group Intervention types Training strategies: any exercise or training-based interventions specifically designed to prevent injury such as neuromuscular warm-up programmes and can include load monitoring/management programming, training design or coaching. Personal protective equipment: can include, but is not limited to helmets, mouthguards, protective eyewear, ankle/knee braces, breast protection and/or soft padded headgear. Policies, rules or laws: policies/rules/laws designed to prevent injury such as eliminating body checking, limiting contact practice and mandating mouthguard use. Other strategies include psychological intervention (eg , coping skills and motivational interviewing), education on multimodal strategies (eg, online concussion prevention education about equipment and coaching and contact training load), general injury prevention intervention not specified (eg, perceptions of injury prevention) No intervention (eg, perceived preventability of injuries and injury risk) Competition level Amateur: recreational, community-level, not defined as elite/elite sub-elite, or participating in local/regional competition. Sub-elite: defined as sub-elite by the study or participating in semi-professional competition. Elite: professional or elite as defined by the study or participating in national or international competition. Athlete age group Adults: aged >18 years (no upper limit on age) Paediatric = aged ≤18 years (no lower limit on age); paper includes children (aged <10) or adolescents (aged 10 to ≤18) By D&I approach: papers were identified as partially (hybrid type 1/2/3) or fully D&I-focussed ( ). A hybrid paper reported both clinical (eg, injury incidence) and D&I research outcomes. Box 3 Definitions of D&I outcomes according to the Quality Enhancement Research initiative (QUERI) Implementation Roadmap and study approach type. Implementation phase The QUERI Implementation Roadmap is a process and determinants model to guide translation of evidence-based interventions into practice. A paper could measure D&I outcomes in any phase. Pre-implementation Outcomes related to planning and dissemination of injury prevention D&I outcome categories: awareness, knowledge, expectations, perceptions (perceived injury risk, preventability, benefits, importance and norms), self-efficacy (belief in one’s ability to implement), intentions or barriers/facilitators/strategies related to dissemination. Implementation Outcomes related to implementation and delivery of injury prevention intervention. D&I outcome categories: feasibility, acceptability, adoption, cumulative utilisation, utilisation frequency, utilisation fidelity, exercise fidelity, duration fidelity, other implementation or delivery outcomes (eg, who delivers and timing of delivery) or barriers/facilitators/strategies related to implementation/delivery. For utilisation frequency: high (>2 times per week), medium (1–2 times per week), and low (<1 time per week) based on reported optimal adherence cut-offs. Sustainment Outcomes related to sustainability and maintenance of injury prevention interventions. D&I outcome categories: reach, maintenance/long-term use, integration of policies/rules/laws, barriers/facilitators/strategies related to sustainment. Study approach Any study design could be included – randomised or non-randomised trials, and any observational quantitative or qualitative, or mixed methods designs. Individual papers were classified according to a “hierarchy of relevance” in relation to D&I objectives: observational-implementation (representing either hybrid/full) hybrid-experimental type 1 (D&I objective is secondary or exploratory) hybrid-experimental type 2 (D&I objective is of equal weight as clinical objective) hybrid-experimental type 3 (D&I objective is prioritised) full D&I experimental papers (D&I objective only) Hybrid effectiveness-implementation experimental studies could include randomised controlled trials, quasi-experimental studies or pre-experimental studies. Type 2 or 3 hybrid and full D&I studies were recognised as relevant for the D&I of evidence-based sports injury prevention. By outcomes . The lead authors (BP, OO, CM, KC and CE) developed a taxonomy of D&I outcome categories ( ) informed by implementation and socio-behavioural models/frameworks. Quantitative and qualitative outcomes could be reported by the users (eg, coaches and players), study personnel (eg, field observations) or other methods (eg, video). Phrases and definitions used by authors (eg, ‘median 12/13 exercises completed each session’) were mapped to the D&I outcome categories (eg, mapped to ‘utilisation fidelity’). Each D&I outcome category was then mapped to the pre-implementation, implementation or sustainment phase of the Quality Enhancement Research Initiative Implementation Roadmap ( ). The number of quantitative papers contributing data in each D&I outcome category and phase was reported. By exposure variables . Any factor associated with any D&I outcome was classified in five categories: socio-demographic, individual, interpersonal, sport system and community, and the number of papers with a quantitative estimate of the effect of the exposure variable was reported. Intervention factors (eg, type, duration and D&I strategy characteristics) were reported narratively. Quantitative and qualitative data were mapped to the same D&I outcomes and/or exposure framework ( ; example extraction is shown in ) and considered alongside quantitative data. Considering the synthesised findings, two authors (CM and BP) determined the presence of qualitative data that can enrich or oppose the quantitative data, and exemplar quotes were chosen to represent the qualitative data. The implementation phase was most represented (n=169, >350 outcomes), whereas the sustainment phase was least represented (n=26, <50 outcomes). Pre-implementation phase Of the 90 papers, 80 had observational-implementation (typically cross-sectional survey) designs. Most (61/90) evaluated athlete/coach perceptions about injury risk, preventability and prevention benefits ( ). Perceptions and attitudes were generally positive. For example, 10/15 papers reported that ≥80% of athletes/coaches perceive injuries to be preventable, and 20/38 papers reported that 50%–90% of athletes/coaches believed that training interventions (eg, exercise and load management) could reduce lower-limb injury risk, and mouthguards could prevent orofacial injuries. 50% to 95% of participants agreed that mouthguards could prevent orofacial injuries. There was agreement about the benefits of PPE to prevent concussion. Coach and athlete confidence to implement was less examined (9/90) and less positive (compared with their perceptions about intervention benefits). Awareness (30/90 papers) of lower-limb injury prevention programmes was moderate (11/30>60% athletes/coaches aware) to high (11/30>80% athletes/coaches aware) but awareness of sport- or organisation-specific programmes (eg, Knakontroll, 11+ and Activate Gaelic) was lower (25%–58%). Of the few papers in low- and middle-income countries, awareness, attitudes and adoption of training interventions and PPE was low (eg, 17%–25% were aware). Qualitative data (15/90) exploring pre-implementation D&I outcomes mostly supported the positive perceptions and attitudes. However, there were some negative athlete/coach perceptions; for example, common themes included that injuries are an inevitable part of sport, and athletes have limited knowledge and struggle to retain information or do not perceive that they are at risk of injury. For females/women/girls, the need to ‘understand the why’ and have equal access to education from experts was emphasised. Implementation phase Most papers with implementation outcomes (n=169) were observational-implementation (104/169) or type 1 hybrid effectiveness-implementation (47/169) studies in the implementation phase. D&I outcomes were predominantly related to adoption (109/169), utilisation frequency (42/169) and cumulative utilisation (33/169). Fidelity D&I outcomes were less commonly reported ( ). Adoption (109 papers, 174 outcomes ). Across all intervention types, adoption rates were spread across high (35/174), medium (n=62/174) and low (n=57/174) categories. In general, PPE had higher adoption rates (51% in high category) than training interventions (30% in high category). Qualitative data suggest that the high rates of PPE adoption may be due to it becoming a ‘habit’ and a ‘part of the uniform’. Cumulative utilisation (33 papers, 42 outcomes) and utilisation frequency (42 papers, 53 outcomes ). Cumulative utilisation was most commonly (29/42) defined as a proportion (%) of completed training intervention sessions, and was mostly medium (19/39) to high (20/39). For the utilisation frequency outcomes, most were medium (ie, 1–2 times per week, 30/53), with few in the high category (more than two times per week: 11/53). Fidelity outcomes . Utilisation fidelity (17/169) and exercise fidelity (20/169) were mostly sub-optimal; only 2/17 papers reported that most (>80%) programme elements were completed, and 2/20 reported that exercises were completed as prescribed (ie, no modifications). Poor acceptability of training interventions (eg, warm-up components) and consequent modifications may contribute to sub-optimal fidelity based on qualitative data. Intervention characteristics: type of exercises (six papers) Six papers evaluated the effect of different types of training interventions on D&I outcomes. Conventional stretching/jogging warm-ups had equivalent D&I to a neuromuscular warm-up programme, whereas the 11+had better D&I outcomes compared with a novel warm-up (eg, a more time-conscious and adaptable programme). Intervention characteristics: acceptability (37 papers) The most reported barriers for training interventions were time (intervention length and competing priorities), lack of perceived relevance/sport-specificity or coach-reported lack of skills/knowledge or education/support/staff to implement (19 papers). Willingness to implement may decrease if the programme is >15 min (94% willing if 15 min, 56% for 20 min and 21% for 30 min). The top facilitators of training interventions were adaptability and ability for progressions/tailoring, sport-specificity, enjoyable, competitive and/partner-based exercises (19 papers). The top reported barriers for PPE were side effects (difficulty breathing/speaking and negative performance effects, 18 papers) and discomfort (15 papers). Dissemination and implementation strategy characteristics (67 experimental papers) Of the 67 experimental papers, 38 were RCTs, 16 had quasi-experimental and 14 had pre-experimental designs. Most (45/67) were hybrid type 1 that compared the effect of injury prevention intervention on standard practice/usual care. The remaining 22/67 had hybrid-experimental type 2 (n=7), hybrid-experimental type 3 (n=4) or full D&I experimental designs (n=11). What dissemination and implementation strategies? Education and/or workshops targeted exclusively at athletes (29/67), coaches (20/67) or both (15/67). There were varying opinions on who was responsible for implementation. Many coaches believed players and/or role models were responsible and critical to buy-in : “Kids will be more likely to follow the role model player than follow the coach that’s harping on at them every day of the week” . Players often reported that coach motivation was critical, and “It would be virtually impossible (to do the injury prevention initiatives) without coach buy-in ”. Parents could play a critical role, particularly for concussion prevention strategies that rely on parents to purchase PPE. Parents’ education level, experiences (eg, contact sport or injury history) and attitudes may influence PPE adoption. Greater team resources and access to health/exercise/medical professionals may enhance D&I outcomes. However, the cost of accessing professionals and/or perceptions (eg, physiotherapist’s role is post-injury rehabilitation) may be barriers. A shared responsibility that fosters athlete, parent, coach, team, health and sport system leadership and culture appears critical. How are dissemination and implementation outcomes measured? D&I outcomes were mostly (55/67) reported in intervention groups only, mostly by athletes (33/67) or coaches/team personnel (23/67). Seven papers validated the coach/trainer D&I outcomes with field observations, and agreement ranged from 60% to 100%. Repeated measures were every session/2–3 time per week (22/67) or weekly (22/67), whereas cross-sectional assessments were typically at the end of the season (13/67). How much supervision and support? (56 experimental papers on training interventions) Most training interventions were incorporated into team practice (44/56), whereas 12/56 had a home/independent programme. Sixteen papers reported implementation supervision by study personnel (n=4 every session, n=6 weekly, n=2 periodic throughout season) or team trainers/health professionals (n=4, every session). Of the three papers evaluating the effect of supervision, all had better D&I outcomes than no supervision; however, only one was statistically significant. Nineteen papers included in-person or online/phone support delivered by study personnel to assist implementation (eg, troubleshoot and provide motivation). The effect of support on D&I outcomes was not evaluated. Discussion This scoping review synthesised the state of quantitative and qualitative evidence to inform current and future research and practice for the D&I of evidence-based injury prevention interventions for female/woman/girl athletes. The 220 included papers involved>4 00 000 participants, across multiple socio-ecological levels and 81 sports, and 49% were female/woman/girl athletes. The under-represented regions (Asia, Africa and South America), populations (eg, Para sport, sub-elite and children), D&I phases (sustainment), and study designs (D&I-focused trials) will direct future research on injury prevention D&I. Papers reported the level of D&I via >650 unique outcomes across the pre-implementation, implementation and sustainment phases, factors associated with D&I and current D&I strategies. Research targets: sociodemographic considerations The lack of research in Para sport, children, sub-elite and non-team sport athletes warrants future funding allocation and capacity building to better understand the unique implementation challenges in these settings. Understanding Para sport injury prevention needs is critical to inform intervention design and evaluation. Sociodemographic factors such as athlete and/or coach sex/gender or age, rurality, ethnic background, education level and school setting may influence implementation ( ) but require further research. Additional implementation barriers (eg, education access, funding opportunities and sports injury perceived importance relative to other health priorities) may exist in lower-income countries and/or more diverse cultural and religious contexts where gender norms, socioeconomic status, race and ethnicity intersect. Early introduction to prevention interventions in children may be important to form habits and change culture, facilitating implementation and sustainment at all ages, similar to school healthy eating initiatives. However, current sports injury prevention interventions are not evaluated in children and may not be relevant for younger players. Since few papers (22/220) used full D&I or hybrid effectiveness implementation type 2/3 designs, the most effective intervention/delivery characteristics (eg, type, education format/timing and level of supervision) remain unclear. Research targets: intervention type and dissemination and implementation outcomes The majority of papers were related to training interventions, and future research should explore the D&I of PPE and policy/rules/laws, which have been more extensively researched in male/men/boy’s contexts. Adoption was the most common D&I outcome assessed; however, it does not equate to how often or how well the intervention is used. More proximal D&I outcomes such as intervention adherence and its dimensions, including cumulative utilisation, utilisation frequency, utilisation fidelity and exercise fidelity, may facilitate dose–response analyses and inform essential programme components and potential adaptations. Practical targets: implementation strategies (who, what and how) Our practical recommendations are for female/women/girls, acknowledging data included mixed sex/gender studies (49% of athletes were female/woman/girl), and more targeted research is required. Fifty-five papers included only female/woman/girls ( ), and 36/165 mixed sex/gender papers disaggregated data ( ). Recommendations could be generalised to male/men/boys’ contexts, and potential female/women/girl-specific considerations are highlighted throughout. The positive perceptions and attitudes and moderate to high levels of adoption and cumulative utilisation identified in this review underpin our practical recommendations. Most D&I strategies included education and/or workshops either in-person (61%) or online (34%), typically delivered in pre-season (70%), by study personnel (63%), to athletes and/or coaches (96%). Few studies used deliverers beyond study personnel, and health/exercise/medical practitioners, coach/athlete educators, champions or technical directors should be involved in future implementation trials. Involving parents, team personnel and sport system administrators in education/workshops may share the responsibility, particularly in the context of under-resourced female/women/girls’ sport settings. Education usually includes lectures/information about injury risk, risk factors (often female sex-based), preventability and intervention efficacy. Given that injuries were perceived as a problem and preventative interventions beneficial, and several female-specific factors are non-modifiable (eg, anatomy), effort should shift to finding solutions to D&I barriers. Reduced lecturing style and more two-way discussions, self-practice, action planning and feedback with intervention users may enhance self-efficacy, adoption and sustained high-fidelity implementation. Pre-season education/workshops were mostly delivered in-person and may address the lack of transfer from better knowledge and positive intention to behaviour change. However, these strategies are resource-intensive, and only one of the two comparative RCTs reported superior D&I outcomes for a more supportive strategy. Although many RCTs had control groups with online materials, between-group D&I outcomes were rarely assessed, and few implementation cost-effectiveness studies exist, providing avenues for future research. In other fields (eg, psychiatry and nursing), online education minimised access and financial barriers with equivalent effectiveness (health/D&I outcomes) to in-person strategies. For PPE, online dissemination strategies may be sufficient, but the most effective platforms (eg, mobile apps, websites and social media) and formats (eg, video animations and infographics) remain unknown. Practical targets: implementation strategies (factors to consider) Practitioners may consider factors associated with D&I (previous injury experience, higher competition level and sport experience) to inform their strategies. Patient stories (ie, their injury experience and importance of prevention) could motivate others and optimise teammates, parents and support staff attitudes/intentions. Better D&I in higher competition levels may mean strategies are required to increase D&I in lower competition and less experienced athletes, for example, tailoring intervention content to amateur settings (eg, leaning into known facilitators for female/women/girls: fun, partner-based activities that are easy for coaches to learn and set up and adaptable to time/sport specific needs) and providing delivery support (eg, supervision and feedback). Female/women/girl athletes in lower competition levels may be more likely to engage in sport for social reasons; however, this should not disbar them from access to best practice injury prevention. Female-specific health factors (eg, breast tenderness and menstrual cycle/pelvic symptoms) may influence athlete participation (eg, reduced attendance or altered technique/performance in contact/impact activity due to symptoms). Raising coach awareness and providing strategies (eg, female health domain language they can use, environmental/personnel supports and technique/exercise modifications) that cater to needs specific to females/women/girls may enhance buy-in and uptake. However, some believe these approaches are unnecessarily progressive, and evaluation of sex/gender specific injury prevention interventions and D&I strategies is required. Practical targets: dissemination strategies Given that positive perceptions and attitudes among female/woman/girl athletes and coaches were associated with better D&I outcomes, pre-implementation initiatives to improve societal awareness and attitudes enhance implementation. Using social media campaigns to increase the uptake of evidence-based prevention interventions is effective (eg, immunology/vaccine uptake). Partnering with sporting organisations can help determine target markets, develop dissemination campaigns, while maintaining evidence-based messaging. Limitations This review only included publications in English, increasing the risk of language and publication bias. Sporting, education and government bodies may be employing injury prevention D&I initiatives without publishing their strategy or outcomes. The number of reviewers involved in screening and data extraction carries a small risk of error in data charting and interpretation. Under-representation of population groups (eg, Para sport, sub-elite and child athletes) limits the generalisability of findings. Conclusion This scoping review synthesised the state of quantitative and qualitative evidence to inform research and practice for the D&I of injury prevention interventions in female/woman/girl athletes. Perceptions and attitudes of coaches were mostly positive, whereas awareness, adoption and cumulative utilisation rates were moderate to high. Key facilitators of D&I include prior injury experience, higher competition level, greater sport experience and positive athlete and coach perceptions, attitudes, intentions and self-efficacy. Strategies to enhance D&I may include education and/or workshops in-person or online, delivered in pre-season by experts. There was limited attention on how well interventions are used or sustained and an unclear effect of supervision on D&I outcomes. Other critical gaps remain, and future research should prioritise under-represented regions (Asia, Africa and South America), populations (eg, studies on Para sport female/woman/girl only, sub-elite and children), D&I phases (sustainment) and study designs (D&I-focused trials). Most papers were focused on athletes and/or coaches. Engaging under-represented levels of the sport system (eg, parents, teachers, health/exercise/medical professionals, trainers and sport/school administrators) may help address the lower rates and understanding of fidelity and long-term sustainability and ultimately reduce injury risk in female/woman/girl athletes.
